questions.question: How does `for range` over a channel stop in Go?
questions.title: Channel range termination
questions.direct_answer: `for value := range ch` repeatedly receives sent values and stops only after `ch` is closed and all buffered values are drained. An open but empty channel makes the loop wait; it does not end. Therefore a finite stream needs a sender-side close, while an intentionally long-lived stream needs cancellation or another return condition around its receive logic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that range termination depends on close, not temporary emptiness.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Ranging over a channel that nobody closes and diagnosing the resulting wait as random deadlock.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain finite stream ownership and distinguish it from long-lived subscription cancellation.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Range performs receives until the channel is closed and drained.
Temporary emptiness makes range wait; it is not an end marker.
Values buffered before close are still delivered.
The sender or sender coordinator closes a finite output stream.
Use select with cancellation for streams that may not close naturally.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A range loop over a channel is shorthand for repeated receives that also check whether the channel is closed. It processes every value sent before closure, including values still buffered, and exits only when the channel is both closed and drained.

An empty open channel is different. More values might arrive later, so the loop blocks waiting rather than ending. This is why `for value := range jobs` can wait forever when all producers return but nobody closes `jobs`. The receiver cannot infer completion from a momentary lack of data.

For example, a producer can create an output channel, send three values, and `defer close(out)`. The consumer ranges without knowing the item count and ends safely after the third value. If several producers share that output, a coordinator closes only after all producers finish.

I use range for a finite stream with clear close ownership. For a subscription or pipeline that can be abandoned early, I add context cancellation and select around blocking operations. Range by itself has no separate timeout or cancel case; it relies entirely on receiving data or observing close.

sections.title: Empty is a moment; closed is permanent
sections.content:
A channel queue can be empty many times during a healthy stream. Treating emptiness as completion would lose later values and create timing-dependent behaviour. Close provides the permanent fact the loop needs: no future send is allowed. The loop can then drain everything already accepted and finish.

This protocol works best when a function returns a receive-only channel that it also arranges to close. The caller receives a self-ending stream, while send ownership stays hidden inside the producer. For long-lived event feeds, termination usually comes from the caller instead, so an explicit context or unsubscribe mechanism belongs in the API.

sections.title: What range sees
sections.content:
| Channel event | Range behaviour |
|---|---|
| Open, value available | Receives value and runs loop body |
| Open, temporarily empty | Waits for a value or close |
| Closed, buffered values remain | Receives remaining values |
| Closed and drained | Exits the loop |
| Nil channel | Waits forever |

questions.question: Why can a Go pipeline leak goroutines when a consumer stops early?
questions.title: Canceling a partially consumed channel pipeline
questions.direct_answer: A pipeline goroutine can leak when it is blocked sending a value that the downstream consumer will never receive. Returning from the consumer does not cancel upstream work. Pass a context or done signal through the stages and select between each potentially blocking send or receive and cancellation, then wait when the owner must confirm shutdown.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reading one result and returning while upstream goroutines remain blocked publishing later results.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why buffering is not a general leak fix and how cancellation reaches every blocking boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A send waits when downstream is not receiving and no buffer slot is free.
A consumer return does not automatically notify upstream goroutines.
Every pipeline stage should observe the same cancellation signal.
Select cancellation around sends as well as long-running receives or I/O.
Buffers can absorb known values but cannot solve unbounded abandonment.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A pipeline stage often loops over input and sends transformed values downstream. If the consumer reads only the first answer and returns, the next send may have no receiver. That stage remains blocked, and it may also prevent earlier stages from sending, retaining goroutines and all data reachable from their stacks.

The fix is an explicit cancellation path. The operation owner creates a context, passes it to every stage, and cancels when it stops consuming. A stage selects between publishing its value and `<-ctx.Done()`, so an abandoned send can return instead of waiting forever. Long-running I/O should use the same context where its API supports it.

For example, a square stage can produce values until the caller accepts the first square. The caller then cancels, and the stage closes its own output as it exits. A coordinator can wait for stage completion when cleanup must be confirmed.

Adding a large buffer is not a general solution because the number of unused values may exceed it, and buffered objects remain retained. A precisely bounded buffer is valid when it covers the entire known protocol; otherwise cancellation is the scalable way to release blocked producers.

sections.title: Backpressure travels upstream
sections.content:
Pipelines form a chain of ownership transfers. When the last consumer stops receiving, its input fills or blocks. The preceding stage can no longer publish, so it stops receiving from its own input, and the blockage moves toward the source. Nothing about a consumer's return is visible to these goroutines unless the protocol carries that information.

A closed cancellation channel provides a broadcast event; `context.Context` packages that event with deadlines and error reasons. Stages should close only their own outbound channels, because cancellation may make them return at different times. The top-level owner cancels; each stage observes, finishes, and closes what it produces.

sections.title: Early exit without and with cancellation
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S[Source] --> T[Transform]
  T -- blocked send --> C[Consumer returned]
  O[Owner cancels context] -. broadcast .-> S
  O -. broadcast .-> T
  S --> X[return and close own output]
  T --> Y[return and close own output]
```
